title: The graph is moved, then asked about
subtitle: Nonlinear functions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: This pattern appears rarely. Learn to recognise it, but do not spend a session on it.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- A graph or an equation is given, and then it is translated up, down, left or right, or reflected across an axis.
- The question asks for a feature of the NEW graph - an intercept, a vertex, a zero, or the equation itself.
- The words 'translated', 'shifted' and 'reflected' are the signal, and the original graph is almost never what is being asked about.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Write down what moved and by how much.
- 2) Apply it to the rule, not to the picture: adding to the whole function moves it up, adding inside the parentheses moves it LEFT, and a minus sign in front flips it across the x-axis.
- 3) Then answer the question about the new rule.
- If the question only wants one feature, track that feature through the move rather than rebuilding the whole equation.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Type the original and the moved version on two lines and look at both.
Dragging a slider on the shift amount makes the direction obvious, which is the part most often reversed.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You move the graph the wrong way horizontally.
Replacing x with (x+3) shifts LEFT, not right, because the input now reaches any given value three units sooner.
The other half of the trap is answering about the original graph after correctly describing the move.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You move the graph the wrong way horizontally.
Replacing x with (x+3) shifts LEFT, not right, because the input now reaches any given value three units sooner.
